title: The fool's three pains
hook: the blind turtle again, and the fool who suffers three ways

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quail held too tight or too loose, and your line, a quail held just right. What came in just before a good mood slipped? Today closes a week. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

Someone at work mentions, in general, that people have been cutting corners on expenses. They don't look at anyone in particular. They don't need to. Somewhere in the room, a face goes hot. The hundred and twenty-ninth discourse is about the fool and the wise person, and it starts with exactly that moment. A fool, the Buddha says, is someone who thinks badly, speaks badly and acts badly. And such a person doesn't have to wait for any afterlife to suffer. They suffer here, in three ways. Today: the fool's three pains.
screen: `NOBODY IN PARTICULAR.` → `A FACE GOES HOT.` → `THREE PAINS, HERE AND NOW.`

segments.voice: Here are the three. First: the fool is sitting in company, and people start talking about the kind of harm he's done. He thinks: they're talking about me. Second: he sees a wrongdoer caught and punished by the king's men, and thinks: that could be me. Third, and this is the image that stays: when he's resting quietly on a chair or a bed, his past wrongs come over him, the text says, the way the shadows of great mountain peaks fall across the land in the evening. Three pains, before anything else happens. The discourse then describes the lower realms after death in vivid, frightening detail. And then it returns to an image you met at the start of this year: the blind turtle. A man throws a yoke with a single hole into the ocean. Winds push it east, west, north, south. A blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years. How likely is it that the turtle puts its neck through that hole? The Buddha says that would happen sooner than the fool, once fallen low, regains a human life. Then the bright side, in mirror image. The wise person thinks, speaks and acts well, and has three joys here and now: easy in company, untroubled at the sight of punishment, and at rest in the evening as good deeds fall over them like those same mountain shadows. Look back at the week: space inside, the real marvel, eighty years in robes, the tamed elephant, sesame and gravel, the light that fades. And now the turtle, surfacing once more.
screen: `THEY'RE TALKING ABOUT ME` · `THAT COULD BE ME` · `SHADOWS OF MOUNTAIN PEAKS` · `THE TURTLE AND THE YOKE` · then, large: `THE TURTLE AND THE YOKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: value your chance. Sit and settle. Picture the wide ocean, and a small wooden yoke drifting on it. Then remember that you're here: alive, human, with a mind that can listen and change. However today is going, in this teaching a human life is a rare chance. Let one breath be a thank you for it. And if a mountain shadow falls over you as you sit, an old regret, just let it be seen, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bala. The fool: fearing they're talked about, fearing they'll be caught, and old wrongs falling over them like mountain shadows at evening. Today's word.
Your line: the turtle and the yoke. Today, use your rare chance on one good act you'd be glad to remember tonight, when the shadows lengthen. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in several traditions cite the blind turtle to stress how precious a human birth is, and Tibetan teachings list 'precious human birth' as the first of four thoughts that turn the mind toward practice.

match.prompt: the fool's three pains: tap the pairs.

myth: in MN 129 the fool's suffering only begins after death
the Buddha describes three pains here and now, before the afterlife is mentioned.
the wise person has three matching joys in this life
easy in company, untroubled at punishment, at rest as good deeds fall over them.
the turtle in the simile comes up once a year
it surfaces once every hundred years, which is why finding the yoke is so unlikely.

fork.setup: you're resting quietly at evening, after a day of harm done to others. what does MN 129 say comes over you?
options: your wrongs, like mountain shadows falling at evening.
fork.reveal: the text's picture is the shadows of great peaks spreading over the land at dusk. for the wise person, the same image is good deeds.

original.note: Pali bala: fool, literally a child or an immature person. MN 129 sets it against pandita, the wise.

trapdoor: what you thought: the fool is punished later, in some hell.
what it means: harm done shows up here and now as three pains: suspicion, fear and the evening shadow of memory.
what a scholar hears: MN 129, the Balapandita Sutta, places the blind turtle simile inside a teaching on kamma and rebirth, the same image found in SN 56.47–48.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 129, Balapandita Sutta (fools and the wise)
Samyutta Nikaya 56.48, Chiggala Sutta (the yoke with a hole)

notes: MN 129 paraphrased. The hell descriptions are summarized, not retold; confirm that's acceptable to a Keeper.
Confirm the three pains and the mountain-shadow simile, and the mirror joys of the wise person.
The turtle callback is to day 347 (SN 56.48). Confirm the yoke has a single hole and the turtle surfaces once in a hundred years in MN 129.

Editor review (days 482–500): replaced the banned 'You know the feeling' opener and stopped telling the listener their face is hot; the practice no longer claims any human life is 'rarer than the turtle finding the yoke' (MN 129 says that of the fool regaining a human birth); cut 'as early Buddhist texts do'.
